title: Animal minds: how animals think, feel and remember

summary.text: Animals think, feel, remember and decide. A crow remembers a face for years, and a dog follows a pointing finger to a hidden treat. Puppies, rats and even bumblebees play, just for fun. You will test what raises water in a glass with the fewest pieces, as rooks did, and learn how scientists test animal minds fairly. Some scientists say we cannot yet know what an animal feels inside, and nobody knows what it is like to be a crow.
summary.art: A crow on a steel railing bending a twig with its beak, a puppy doing a play bow beside it, and a child watching both with a notebook.

intro.hook: You probably know the story of the thirsty crow. It drops pebbles into a pot until the water rises. Do you think a real crow could do that? Or is it just a story?
intro.text: In 2009, two scientists in England tested it. They gave rooks, a kind of crow, a tall tube of water. A worm floated on the water, too low for a beak to reach. Stones lay next to the tube. The rooks picked up stones and dropped them in, one by one. The water rose, and they ate the worm. They even chose the big stones first. So the story was right: a real bird can solve this problem. In this unit you will find out what else animals learn, remember and work out.
intro.art: A black rook beside a tall clear tube of water, a stone in its beak, a worm floating near the top, and a small pile of pebbles beside the tube.

outcomes: I can give true examples of animals that play, learn and remember.
I can explain how a crow uses a tool, and how a chimpanzee uses one.
I can explain how dogs read our faces and follow pointing.
I can run a fair test, and change only one thing at a time.
I can explain why a test must be 'blind', using the story of Clever Hans the horse.
I can say what scientists agree on about animal minds, and what they still argue about.
I can explain that a brain is made of neurons that pass tiny electric signals. I know a small brain can still be very clever.

terms.meaning: The part of you that thinks, feels, learns and remembers. Nobody can see a mind directly. We can only see what it does.
terms.example: You decide to pick the mango, not the banana. Your mind made that choice.
terms.art: A child choosing between a mango and a banana, with a soft glow around the child's head.

terms.meaning: Changing what you do because of what happened before.
terms.example: A dog runs to the gate when it hears the gate click. It learned that the click means someone is coming home.
terms.art: A dog running towards a gate as it clicks open.

terms.meaning: Keeping something you learned, so you can use it later.
terms.example: You remember where you hid your sweets last week.
terms.art: A child reaching into a hidden spot behind a book for a sweet.

terms.meaning: Something an animal does without being taught. It is born ready to do it.
terms.example: A baby turtle walks towards the sea the moment it hatches. Nobody shows it the way.
terms.art: A tiny turtle hatchling crawling across sand towards the waves.

terms.meaning: Doing something just for fun, again and again, when you are safe and relaxed. It does not get you food or shelter right away.
terms.example: Two puppies chase each other and roll about, but nobody gets hurt.
terms.art: Two puppies tumbling together on grass, tails wagging.

terms.meaning: An object you use to help you do a job. It is not part of your body.
terms.example: A spoon is a tool for eating. A twig is a tool for a crow fishing out a grub.
terms.art: A spoon next to a twig held in a crow's beak.

terms.meaning: Finding a new way to get what you want, when the usual way does not work.
terms.example: The ball is under the bed and your arm is too short. You use a broom to reach it.
terms.art: A child lying on the floor reaching under a bed with a broom to pull out a ball.

terms.meaning: The body part inside the head that thinks, feels and remembers. It takes in messages from the senses and sends out messages that move the body.
terms.example: When you see a ball coming, your eyes send a message to your brain. Your brain tells your hands to catch it.
terms.art: A simple side view of a child's head with the brain shown, an arrow from the eyes to the brain, and an arrow from the brain to a hand catching a ball.

terms.meaning: A tiny messenger cell in the brain and body. Neurons pass tiny electric signals to each other.
terms.example: Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. A honeybee's brain has about one million.
terms.art: A branching neuron cell with a spark of signal travelling along it.

terms.meaning: A feeling, like happy, scared or angry. It changes your face and body.
terms.example: When you are scared, your heart beats fast and you want to run.
terms.art: Three children's faces: happy, scared and angry.

terms.meaning: What a body shows about feelings, without words.
terms.example: A dog with its tail tucked under and ears flat is scared.
terms.art: A dog with a tucked tail and flat ears, next to a relaxed dog with a loose wagging tail.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing, and keep everything else the same.
terms.example: To test big stones against small ones, use the same glass and the same water each time.
terms.art: Two identical glasses of water side by side, one with big stones and one with small stones.

terms.meaning: A test where the person giving it does not know the answer. Then they cannot give away the answer by mistake.
terms.example: One friend hides a coin under a cup while you look away. Now your brother tries to find it. You cannot give him clues, because you do not know where it is either.
terms.art: A child with eyes covered while another child hides a coin under one of three steel cups.

terms.meaning: What you saw or measured that shows an idea is true or false.
terms.example: The rook dropped stones and ate the worm. That is evidence that it solved the problem.
terms.art: A notebook with a tick next to a drawing of a rook and a tube.

terms.meaning: A person who watches animals very carefully, and tests what they can do. This science is called ethology.
terms.example: Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees in Tanzania for many years.
terms.art: A woman sitting quietly in a forest with binoculars and a notebook, a chimpanzee in the trees.

terms.meaning: A test to see if an animal knows the animal in a mirror is itself. A mark is put on its body where it can only see it in the mirror.
terms.example: A child with a sticker on their forehead looks in the mirror and touches their own forehead.
terms.art: A toddler touching a sticker on their forehead while looking in a mirror.

explanations.description: Animals think, feel, remember and decide. We know it from what they do: a crow chooses a stone, and a dog greets you with its whole body. Nobody can see a thought directly, in an animal or in a person. With a friend too, you see what they do and say, and you know their mind from that. Some scientists say this is not enough for animals, and that every claim needs a careful test.
examples: A cat waits by the kitchen door at the same time every evening. It remembers when dinner comes, and it chooses to wait there.
A crow drops a hard nut onto a road, waits for a car to crack it, then flies down to eat.

perspectives.who: Rene Descartes, a French thinker, in 1637
perspectives.explanation: Animals are like very clever machines, like a clock. They move and make sounds, but they do not think or feel anything inside.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, an English scientist, in 1871 and 1872
perspectives.explanation: Humans are animals too, and we come from the same family tree. So other animals have the same kinds of feelings and thinking as us, but in different amounts.

Many animals clearly learn, remember and solve problems. We can test those things. What an animal feels inside is much harder to test. So they say: test carefully, and choose the simplest explanation that fits.

explanations.art: Three panels: a clockwork bird with gears, Darwin's branching family tree with a child and a crow on two branches, and a scientist with a notebook watching a dog.
explanations.context: This card is about what a mind is, and how we can know that animals think and feel.

explanations.definition: Learning is changing what you do because of what happened before.
explanations.description: Almost every animal learns, from a worm to an elephant. The simplest learning is noticing that one thing comes before another. Around 1900, Ivan Pavlov, a Russian scientist, found that dogs learned to drool at a sound that came before food. Another kind is learning by trying. Edward Thorndike, an American scientist, put cats in puzzle boxes in 1898. Each time, a cat escaped a little faster. Animals also learn by watching others, just as you learn by watching a cousin.
examples: Your dog runs to the kitchen when it hears the fridge open.
Pigeons in Japan learned to tell paintings by Monet from paintings by Picasso. Shigeru Watanabe and his team showed this in 1995.
Young crows watch older crows, and learn which people are dangerous.
explanations.art: Three panels: a dog at an open fridge, a pigeon pecking a button below a painting, a young crow watching an older crow on a wall.
explanations.context: This card explains learning, one of the things this unit shows animals can do.

explanations.definition: Memory is keeping what you learned, so you can use it later.
explanations.description: Some birds hide food and come back for it months later. A Clark's nutcracker, a bird of the American mountains, hides many thousands of pine seeds in autumn. It finds a lot of them in winter, under snow. In 1998, Nicola Clayton and Anthony Dickinson showed that scrub jays remember what they hid, where they hid it, and when. Crows also remember faces. Elephants remember the calls of their family and friends.
examples: In the United States, John Marzluff's team caught a few crows while wearing a mask. For years after, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, even crows that had never been caught.

In Kenya, Karen McComb and her team played elephant calls to elephant families in 2001. Families with an older grandmother elephant as leader were better at telling friends' calls from strangers' calls.
explanations.art: A grey bird pushing a pine seed into soil, then the same bird in snow digging it up, with a dotted line joining the two pictures.
explanations.context: This card explains memory in animals, with true examples from birds and elephants.

explanations.definition: Play is doing something again and again just for fun, when you are safe and relaxed. It does not get food or shelter right away.
explanations.description: Gordon Burghardt, an American scientist, wrote down clear signs that tell play apart from other things animals do. Using those signs, scientists have found play in many animals. Puppies, kittens and goats play. Rats play chase, and they make a happy chirp when tickled. The chirp is too high for us to hear without a special microphone. Jaak Panksepp, an American scientist, studied this from the late 1990s. Octopuses have pushed floating bottles around their tank again and again. In 2022, scientists in London found that bumblebees rolled little wooden balls, even with no food as a reward.
examples: A puppy bows with its front legs down and its tail up. This 'play bow' means 'let's play, this is not a real fight'.
Young goats jump and twist in the air, just for fun.
Bumblebees rolled wooden balls many times, for nothing but the rolling. The young bees rolled them the most.
explanations.art: A puppy in a play bow, a rat being gently tickled with a fingertip, and a fuzzy bumblebee pushing a tiny yellow ball.
explanations.context: This card explains play, and the true animals scientists have seen playing.

explanations.description: Play uses energy and can be risky. So why do animals do it? Scientists have several ideas, and they still argue. Most think play does more than one job.
examples: Lion cubs pounce on each other's tails.
Children make up rules for a game, then change them.

perspectives.explanation: Play is practice for real life. A kitten pouncing on a ball is practising hunting. A puppy wrestling is practising fighting, without getting hurt.
Play builds friendships. Animals that play together learn to trust each other, and to take turns.
Play trains the body and brain to cope with surprises. When you fall over in a game, you learn to get up quickly.
Some scientists say play may simply feel good, and that is reason enough. The bumblebees rolled balls with no prize at all.

explanations.art: Two lion cubs wrestling, one pouncing on the other's tail, with a mother lion watching.
explanations.context: Scientists agree that many animals play. This card is about why they do it, which is still argued about.

explanations.definition: A tool is an object an animal uses to help it do a job. It is not part of its own body.
explanations.description: People once said only humans use tools. In 1960, Jane Goodall watched a chimpanzee in Tanzania. She named him David Greybeard. He pulled a grass stem, stripped off its leaves and poked it into a termite mound. Termites grabbed the stem, and he ate them. Since then, scientists have found many tool users. New Caledonian crows, from islands in the Pacific Ocean, make hooks from forked twigs and cut tools from stiff leaves. They use them to pull grubs out of holes. In 2002, a crow called Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a little bucket of food out of a tube.
examples: In Africa, Egyptian vultures throw stones at ostrich eggs to crack them open. Jane Goodall and Hugo van Lawick reported this in 1966. These vultures live in India too.
Sea otters float on their backs and crack shellfish on a stone.
Some scientists think mugger crocodiles in India balance sticks on their snouts in the nesting season, to trick birds looking for twigs. Others are not sure yet.
explanations.art: A chimpanzee poking a stripped grass stem into a tall termite mound, termites clinging to the stem.
explanations.context: This card explains tool use, one of the main things this unit is about.

explanations.definition: Problem solving is finding a new way to get what you want, when the usual way does not work.
explanations.description: About a hundred years ago, Wolfgang Kohler, a German scientist, put bananas out of reach of chimpanzees. One chimpanzee, Sultan, fitted two short sticks together to make one long one, and pulled the fruit in. In 2009, Christopher Bird and Nathan Emery gave rooks a tube of water with a worm floating too low to reach. The rooks dropped in stones until they could reach it. They picked big stones first. Later, New Caledonian crows passed similar tests, and chose sinking stones over floating things.
examples: A crow drops a hard nut onto a road, so a car cracks it.
A cat learns to pull down a door handle with its paw.
explanations.art: A chimpanzee fitting two short sticks together to reach bananas lying on the ground outside its cage.
explanations.context: This card explains problem solving, and two famous tests of it with chimpanzees and rooks.

explanations.definition: Dogs notice where people look and point, and they can tell some human feelings from faces.
explanations.description: If you point at one of two bowls, most pet dogs go to the bowl you pointed at. Brian Hare and his team showed this in 2002. Dogs even do better at this than chimpanzees. In 2015, scientists in Vienna showed dogs photos of human faces. The dogs learned to tell happy faces from angry ones, even for people they had never met. In India, Anindita Bhadra and her team at IISER Kolkata tested street dogs that nobody had trained. Many of them followed a pointing finger to a bowl.
examples: Your dog looks at your face, then at the ball, then back at you.
A street dog moves away from someone shouting, and towards someone kneeling and speaking softly.
explanations.art: A girl pointing at one of two upturned steel bowls, and a brown dog looking where she points.
explanations.context: This card explains how dogs read human faces and pointing, which this unit covers.

explanations.concept: Why dogs are so good with people
explanations.description: Dogs came from wolves that began living near people many thousands of years ago. Scientists argue about why dogs read us so well.
examples: Wolf pups raised by people follow pointing less well than dog puppies do, in many tests.
Dogs who live in houses get lots of practice watching people.

perspectives.explanation: Over thousands of years, the dogs that were best at reading people did best living with people. So reading people became part of being a dog, from birth.

perspectives.who: Monique Udell, Clive Wynne and others
perspectives.explanation: Dogs learn it while growing up with people. Wolves raised closely with people can learn to follow pointing too.
Probably both. Dogs are born ready to watch people, and living with people makes them better at it.

explanations.art: A wolf and a dog side by side, both looking up at a person's pointing hand.
explanations.context: Dogs are very good at reading people. This card is about why, which scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Clever Hans: the horse who read faces
explanations.definition: The Clever Hans effect is when an animal or person picks up tiny clues from someone who knows the answer, without anyone meaning to give them.
explanations.description: Around 1904, a horse in Berlin called Hans seemed to do sums. He tapped his hoof to give the answer. Then a scientist called Oskar Pfungst tested him carefully. He wrote a book about it in 1907. Hans was right only when the person asking knew the answer, and when Hans could see them. As Hans tapped, the asker tensed up. When he reached the right number, the asker relaxed a tiny bit. Hans saw it and stopped. So Hans could not do sums. But he could read tiny changes in people's faces and bodies, which is clever in its own way.
examples: Scientists who test animals now often make the test 'blind'. The person in the room does not know the answer.
A dog may 'find' a hidden toy because its owner glances at the hiding place.
explanations.art: A horse in a Berlin courtyard tapping its hoof on a board of numbers, with a man in a hat watching closely.
explanations.context: This card tells the true story of a horse that seemed to do maths, and what it teaches about fair tests of animal minds.

explanations.definition: A brain is made of tiny messenger cells called neurons. Neurons pass signals by moving charged atoms, called ions, in and out.
explanations.description: In a brain, every thought, memory and feeling comes with neurons sending tiny electric signals. The signal is made by charged atoms of sodium and potassium, the same atoms that are in salt and bananas. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian scientist, helped count them. A honeybee has about one million neurons in a brain smaller than a sesame seed. In 2016, scientists found that bird brains pack neurons very tightly. A crow's small brain has about as many neurons in its thinking part as some monkeys have. So brain size alone does not tell you how clever an animal is.
examples: Your brain uses about a fifth of all the energy your body uses, even while you sleep.
An elephant's brain is more than three times as heavy as yours.
A crow's brain is about the size of a walnut, but crows make tools.
explanations.art: A walnut, a lemon and a small papaya on a kitchen counter labelled crow, dog and human by little drawings, with a zoom-in circle showing tiny neurons sparking.
explanations.context: This card zooms in to what thinking is made of: neurons, atoms and electricity.

explanations.concept: A mind with eight arms: the octopus
explanations.description: An octopus has about 500 million neurons. About two thirds of them are in its arms, not its head. Each arm can feel, taste and grab on its own. Our last shared ancestor with the octopus was a small worm-like animal, more than 500 million years ago. So clever minds came about at least twice, separately, on two very different branches of life. Peter Godfrey-Smith, a philosopher who dives with octopuses, wrote about this in his book Other Minds, in 2016. What it feels like to be an octopus, nobody knows.
examples: Octopuses in aquariums have unscrewed jar lids to get crabs inside.
Some octopuses carry coconut shell halves and hide inside them.
explanations.art: An octopus on the sea floor holding two halves of a coconut shell, one arm curling off to explore a rock on its own.
explanations.context: This card goes deep: a very different kind of clever animal, and what it tells us about how minds came to be.

explanations.description: Animals feel. A dog shows joy with its whole body, and a hurt fish avoids the place where it was hurt. Many scientists agree, at least for mammals and birds. Others say we cannot yet test what an animal feels inside, so we should not be sure.
examples: A dog greets you with its whole body wagging.
Elephants touch and smell the bones of dead elephants for a long time.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, in his book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, 1872
perspectives.explanation: Animals show fear, anger and joy with their faces and bodies, much as we do. So they probably feel them.

perspectives.who: Conwy Lloyd Morgan, an English scientist, in 1894
perspectives.explanation: Do not say an animal is thinking or feeling something complicated, if a simpler explanation fits. Be careful, and test first.

perspectives.who: Many scientists, in the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness, 2024
perspectives.explanation: There is strong evidence that mammals and birds have feelings. There is a real chance that fish, octopuses, crabs and insects do too. It would be wrong to ignore this.
Behaviour can look like feeling without any feeling inside. A robot can cry out when hit. We need better tests before we say an insect feels.

explanations.art: An elephant gently touching an old elephant bone with its trunk while two others stand close.
explanations.context: This card is about animal feelings, and the different views scientists hold about them.

agreed.text: Many animals learn from what happens to them.
agreed.evidence: Dogs, cats, rats, pigeons, bees and even worms change what they do after rewards or shocks. Scientists have tested this thousands of times.

agreed.text: Many animals remember for a long time.
agreed.evidence: Jays find hidden food months later. Crows scolded a 'dangerous' mask for years in John Marzluff's study.

agreed.text: Humans are not the only tool users.
agreed.evidence: Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees fish for termites in 1960. Crows, vultures, otters and many others use tools too.
Play has been seen in mammals and birds, and there is evidence for it in octopuses and bumblebees.

agreed.text: Dogs follow human pointing and notice human faces.
agreed.evidence: Pet dogs, and many untrained street dogs in India, go to the bowl a person points at in careful tests.

challenging.claim: Only humans make and use tools.
challenging.who: Many people before 1960. Some books still say it.
challenging.for: No other animal builds cars, phones or houses like ours.
challenging.against: Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees make tools from grass stems in 1960. Her teacher Louis Leakey wrote that we must now redefine 'tool', redefine 'man', or accept chimpanzees as humans. Crows bend hooks too.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that tools make humans special, and why scientists dropped it.

challenging.claim: Animals are machines with no feelings inside.
challenging.who: Rene Descartes, a French thinker, in 1637, and many people after him.
challenging.for: We cannot see feelings, only behaviour. A machine could act as if it were in pain.
challenging.against: Animals have the same brain chemicals for fear and pleasure as we do. They choose to avoid pain and seek comfort. Most scientists now think at least mammals and birds feel.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that animals are just machines.

challenging.claim: A bigger brain always means a cleverer animal.
challenging.who: Many of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: Humans have big brains for their size, and we do many clever things.
challenging.against: Elephants and whales have bigger brains than us. Crows have tiny brains but make tools, because their neurons are packed tightly. Bees learn a lot with a brain smaller than a sesame seed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether brain size tells us how clever an animal is.

challenging.claim: A dog that looks 'guilty' knows it did something wrong.
challenging.for: The dog lowers its head and tail, and won't meet your eyes, after it chews a chappal.
challenging.against: In 2009, Alexandra Horowitz tested this. Dogs looked most 'guilty' when the owner scolded them, even if the dog had done nothing wrong. The look may mean 'please don't be angry', not 'I feel guilty'.
challenging.context: This card is about the 'guilty look' of dogs, and what a careful test found.

challenging.claim: The mirror test shows which animals know themselves.
challenging.who: Gordon Gallup, an American scientist, who invented the test in 1970.
challenging.for: Chimpanzees, an Asian elephant called Happy, and magpies touched a mark they could only see in a mirror.
challenging.against: Dogs mostly fail the mirror test, but they know their own smell. In 2017, Alexandra Horowitz showed dogs sniff a changed smell of their own longer. Animals that do not use eyes much may need a different test. A small fish, the cleaner wrasse, seemed to pass in 2019, and scientists are still arguing about what that means.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous test of whether animals know themselves, and whether it is fair.

challenging.claim: Fish and insects cannot feel pain.
challenging.for: Their brains are very different from ours, and much smaller.
challenging.against: Fish rub a sore lip and avoid a place where they were hurt. Bees and crabs also act in pain-like ways in some tests. Many scientists now say we should be careful and kind.
challenging.context: This card is about whether fish and insects feel pain, which is still argued about.

big_questions.q: If you can never see inside another being's mind, how do you know your friend has feelings?
big_questions.hint: What does your friend do that tells you how they feel?

big_questions.q: Is a crow that makes a hook clever, even though it cannot read?
big_questions.hint: Are there different ways to be clever? What is a crow clever at that you are not?

big_questions.q: What is it like to be a bat that 'sees' with sound, or an octopus that tastes with its arms?
big_questions.hint: Close your eyes. Tap a spoon and listen. Could you find the wall just by sound?

big_questions.q: If an animal can feel scared or happy, how should we treat it?
big_questions.hint: Think of a street dog, a hen and a goat. Does it change how you would treat them?

big_questions.q: Why do animals play, when play does not get them food?
big_questions.hint: What do you learn when you play a game with friends?

big_questions.q: Is a thought made of anything? What is a memory made of?
big_questions.hint: Neurons pass tiny electric signals made by moving atoms. Is a memory just atoms, or something more?

big_questions.q: A horse called Hans fooled clever people for years. How can we make sure we are not fooling ourselves when we test animals?
big_questions.hint: What if the person giving the test does not know the answer?

big_questions.q: Could a computer or robot ever really feel? How would we know?
big_questions.hint: Can you tell from the outside whether something feels?

big_questions.q: If crows and octopuses got clever on their own, could minds grow anywhere in the universe?
big_questions.hint: Crows and octopuses come from very different branches of life.

big_questions.q: Who decides which animals count as clever, and why do we often pick the ones most like us?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a test made for humans might be unfair to a dog that thinks with its nose.

story.title: The Horse Who Watched Faces
story.note: Clever Hans was a real horse in Berlin, owned by a retired teacher called Wilhelm von Osten. In 1904 crowds came to see him, and Oskar Pfungst tested him and showed he was reading tiny movements of the people asking. Lotte, her father and the scenes in the stable are made up.
text: In Berlin, more than a hundred years ago, there was a courtyard with tall grey walls. In the courtyard lived a horse who could count. Or so everybody said.

His name was Hans. He was a tall black stallion with a white star on his face. Every afternoon, his owner, an old teacher called Herr von Osten, led him out into the yard. People crowded at the gate in their best hats. Herr von Osten would ask, 'Hans, what is three and two?' And Hans would lift his right front hoof and tap the cobbles. One, two, three, four, five. Then he stopped. The crowd clapped and gasped. Newspapers called him Clever Hans.

Lotte was nine, and she knew Hans better than anyone. Her father was the groom who brushed him and fed him. Lotte carried the oats in a bucket that banged against her knees. She knew which spot behind Hans's ear he liked scratched. She knew he snorted when she was late. And she knew something else, which nobody had asked her about. Hans always knew when she was sad.

On the day her best friend moved away to Hamburg, Lotte had come into the stable with her face stiff. She had not cried. She had not said a word. But Hans had turned from his hay and pushed his big soft nose into her shoulder, and kept it there. 'How did you know?' she had whispered. Hans had only blinked.

Then the scientists came. There were thirteen of them at first, with notebooks and pocket watches. They watched Hans for days. They looked for tricks, for signals, for strings. They found none. Herr von Osten was not cheating, they said. He truly believed his horse could think like a schoolboy.
But one young man stayed on. His name was Oskar Pfungst. He had round glasses and a careful, quiet voice. He did not clap when Hans got a sum right. He wrote everything down.
'May I ask Hans a question,' he said one morning, 'that I do not know the answer to myself?'
Herr von Osten frowned. 'What a strange thing to ask.'
Pfungst wrote a number on a card. He did not look at it. He held it up in front of Hans, face out, so only the horse could see it. 'Tap the number, Hans.'
Hans tapped. And tapped. And tapped. He tapped past five, past ten, past twenty. He did not stop. The courtyard went very quiet. Lotte felt her cheeks go hot, as if she were the one getting it wrong.
Pfungst turned the card round. It said seven. He wrote something in his notebook.

For days he tested. When the person asking knew the answer, Hans was almost always right. When the person asking did not know, Hans was almost always wrong. When Hans wore big blinkers and could not see the person's face, he was lost.
'So he is a fraud,' said a man at the gate, and spat. 'A horse that cannot do sums.'

Herr von Osten went grey. He stopped coming down to the yard. Lotte's father brushed Hans without humming. The crowds thinned to nobody. Lotte sat on an upturned bucket and stared at the horse, and the horse stared back.

Then Pfungst did one more thing, and Lotte was there to see it. He stood in front of Hans and asked a sum. As Hans began to tap, Pfungst did not speak or move his hands. But when Hans reached the right number, Pfungst let his head lift, the tiniest bit. It was less than the width of a fingernail. Hans stopped.
Pfungst did it again with a wrong number. He lifted his head at four, when the answer was six. Hans stopped at four.

'There,' Pfungst said softly, and he looked almost happy. 'Every person who asks him leans forward a little while he taps. When he reaches the answer, they relax. They do not even know they do it. But he sees it. Every time.'
Lotte stood up off her bucket.

She thought of the crowd at the gate, leaning, holding their breath, then letting it out in a rush. She thought of Herr von Osten's eyebrows rising. She thought of her own stiff face on the day her friend went to Hamburg, and the warm nose pushing into her shoulder.

Hans could not do sums. That was true. But he had been doing something else all along, something none of them had thought to test. He had been reading them. He had been watching hundreds of strangers' faces, every afternoon, and catching changes too small for the people themselves to notice. He knew when they were waiting. He knew when they were pleased. He knew when a girl was sad, and said nothing.
'They are calling him stupid,' Lotte said to Pfungst. She was surprised to hear her own voice. 'But none of them could do what he does.'
Pfungst looked at her for a long moment over his round glasses. Then he wrote something in his notebook, and he did not show her what.
That evening Lotte brought the oats. She did not hurry. She stood in front of Hans and let herself feel what she felt, which was a mix of sorry and proud and glad. She did not say anything.
Hans lowered his head and blew warm air into her hands. Then he waited, the way he always did, watching her face to see what she would do next.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Hans could not do sums, but he could read tiny changes in human faces and bodies, smaller than people knew they were making. The crowd saw only the trick they expected and missed the real cleverness. Animal minds are often clever in ways we do not think to test. The story also hides the idea of a blind test: Pfungst found the truth by asking a question he did not know the answer to himself.
ask: In the story, why did Hans tap and tap when Oskar Pfungst held up a number he had not looked at?
What tiny thing did the people asking Hans do when he reached the right number?
The man at the gate said Hans was a fraud. Lotte said none of them could do what Hans did. Who do you agree with, and why?
How did Hans know Lotte was sad, when she had not said a word?
Has an animal ever seemed to know how you were feeling? What did it do?
