games.title: True or Tall Tale?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about animal minds. Each card says something about what an animal can do. Players decide whether it is true, with evidence, or a tall tale.

printables.title: 22 claim cards to cut out
items: Crows can recognise one human face and remember it for years.
A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds.
Bumblebees roll little balls just for fun.
Dogs can tell a happy human face from an angry one in photos.
An elephant never forgets anything at all.
Rats make a happy chirp when they are tickled.
A crow bent a straight wire into a hook to get food.
Chimpanzees poke grass stems into termite mounds to fish for termites.
Pigeons learned to tell paintings by Monet from paintings by Picasso.
A horse called Hans really could do sums.
Bigger brains always mean cleverer animals.
Octopuses have most of their neurons in their arms.
Rooks drop stones into water to raise it and reach a floating worm.
Young crows learn who is dangerous by watching older crows.
A dog that looks guilty always knows it did something wrong.
Jays remember what food they hid, where, and when.
Many street dogs in India follow a pointing finger, even untrained.
TEST IT: hide a coin under one of three cups. Can someone find it by watching your face?
TEST IT: point at something in the room without saying a word. Does everyone look where you point?
TEST IT: everyone shut your eyes and point to where the door is. Then open them. Whose memory was right?
TEST IT: make a happy face, then an angry face, at the nearest person. Can they name each feeling without words?

printables.title: Two playing mats
items: TALL TALE: a test showed it is not true

rules: Cut out the 22 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Everyone says TRUE or TALL TALE. Then the reader puts the card on a mat.
Check the answer in the app or the answer list. If you were right, take one evidence token.
If you can say how scientists found out, take one more token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. Everyone who joins in gets a token.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

setup.art: Two paper mats on a floor, one with a tick and a magnifying glass, one with a cloud and a question mark, a face-down pile of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the TRUE and TALL TALE mats. Put the cards face down.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while two others point to the mats.
setup.caption: 2. Read the top card. Everyone says TRUE or TALL TALE.

setup.art: A small pile of paper circles with a magnifying glass drawn on each, being handed to a child.
setup.caption: 3. Right answer: one token. Say how we know: one more.

flow.do: 1. Lay the TRUE and TALL TALE mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 22 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Each card says something about an animal's mind. Some are true, and scientists have tested them. Some are tall tales that people believe, but tests showed they are wrong.
flow.kid: Put the two mats down: TRUE and TALL TALE. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, decide: true, or a tall tale?
flow.context: This is the first step of True or Tall Tale?, a card game about what animals can really do. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds'. Play it as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds.' True, or tall tale?
flow.kid: Practice card: a goldfish forgets everything after three seconds. True or tall tale? Tap your answer.

ask.q: How could you test a goldfish's memory?
good: Feed it in one corner every day and see if it swims there.
Teach it a signal and check days later.

check.q: A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds. True or tall tale?
options: True
Tall tale
check.why: It is a tall tale. Goldfish have been trained to swim to a sound or a light for food, and remembered it weeks or months later. Picking 'true' usually means trusting a saying we have heard many times, instead of asking what a test showed.

flow.context: This is a practice round of True or Tall Tale?, a card game about animal minds.

flow.do: Take turns drawing cards. After each card, read the answer from the answer list in the app. Hand out tokens.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card. Everyone say true or tall tale. Now, how do you think scientists found out?
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it out. True or tall tale? Then say how scientists could test it.
flow.parent: Answers. TRUE: crows remember faces, bumblebees roll balls, dogs tell happy from angry faces, rats chirp when tickled, the wire hook, termite fishing, pigeons and paintings, octopus arms, rooks and stones, young crows learning, jays remembering, street dogs pointing. TALL TALE: goldfish three seconds, only humans make tools, elephants never forget anything, Hans could do sums, bigger brain always cleverer, guilty look always means guilt. Elephants do have very good memories, but no animal remembers everything.

check.q: Card: 'A horse called Hans really could do sums.' What is the truth?
options: True: he tapped the right answers
Tall tale: he read tiny changes in people's faces
True, but only for small numbers
check.why: Hans got the answers right only when the asker knew the answer and Hans could see them. The asker relaxed a tiny bit at the right number, and Hans stopped. Picking 'true' means trusting what we see on the outside, without a blind test.

flow.context: This is the main part of True or Tall Tale?, a card game where players decide which claims about animal minds are true.

flow.do: When you draw a TEST IT card, stop and do the test together.
flow.say: A test card! Let's all try it now. Then let's talk about what happened.
flow.kid: Test card! Do the test together. What happened? Was it a surprise?
flow.think: Which card surprised you most? Why did you believe the tall tales at first?
flow.context: This step of True or Tall Tale? is about the TEST IT cards, where players try a small test about minds.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then ask your child for one claim, one piece of evidence and one reason.
flow.say: Pick one true card. What does it show? What is the evidence? Why does that evidence make it true?
flow.kid: Count your tokens! Then pick one true card. Say what it shows, and how we know.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: crows remember faces. Evidence: crows scolded the mask for years. Why: they must have kept the face in memory.
flow.context: This is the last step of True or Tall Tale?. It ends with the child saying what they think, what the evidence is, and why.

games.title: Read My Face
games.context: This is a guessing game about faces and feelings. One player makes a feeling with only their face and body, and the others guess it. It shows how dogs, horses and people read faces.
rules: Shuffle the feeling cards and put them face down.
The face-maker takes a card and does not show it. They show the feeling with face and body only. No sounds, no words.
The others guess. The first right guess wins a point. The face-maker also wins a point.
In round two, the face-maker may only use their face, hands behind their back.
In round three, the face-maker may only use their body. They turn their face away.
After the game, talk about which round was easiest, and why.

setup.art: A small pile of cards face down, each with a simple face symbol on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the feeling cards. Put them face down.

setup.art: A child making a big scared face with hands up, while others point and guess.
setup.caption: 2. Show the feeling with your face and body, with no words.

setup.art: A child with their face turned away, shoulders slumped and hanging their arms, while others guess 'sad'.
setup.caption: 3. Round three: show it with your body only.

flow.do: Shuffle the 16 feeling cards. Explain the rules.
flow.say: In this game you show a feeling without any words. Dogs and horses watch our faces all the time. Let's see how good we are at it.
flow.kid: Take a card. Don't show anyone. Show the feeling with your face. No words!
flow.context: This is the first step of Read My Face, a game about showing and reading feelings without words.

flow.do: Play three rounds. Round one: face and body. Round two: face only. Round three: body only, face turned away.
flow.say: Round one, use your whole body. Round two, only your face. Round three, turn your face away and use only your body.
flow.kid: Round one: face and body. Round two: face only. Round three: body only. Which is hardest?

check.q: In Read My Face, which round is usually hardest to guess?
options: Face and body together
Face only
Body only, with the face turned away
check.why: We read most feelings from faces, especially eyes and mouths. Dogs look at our faces for the same reason. Picking 'face and body together' is often a slip: that round has the most clues, so it is usually easiest.

flow.context: This is the main part of Read My Face, a game about feelings and faces.

flow.do: Talk about the game. Then tell your child about dogs reading faces.
flow.say: Scientists in Vienna showed dogs photos of happy and angry human faces. The dogs learned to tell them apart. They could even do it with people they had never met. How do you think a dog does that?
flow.kid: Dogs can tell a happy face from an angry face. How do you think they do it?

ask.q: What part of the face tells you most?

flow.context: This step of Read My Face links the game to the science of dogs reading human faces.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now about reading faces? What did you see in the game? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: faces show feelings best. What I saw: we guessed almost every face, but body-only was hard. Why: eyes and mouths change most with feelings.
flow.context: This is the last step of Read My Face. The child says what they think, what they saw, and why.

experiments.title: The Thirsty Crow Test: what raises the water best?
experiments.context: This is the thirsty crow test. You drop things into a glass of water, like the crow in the old story, and count how many it takes to raise the water to a line. Real rooks and crows have passed this test.
experiments.question: Which raises the water to the line with the fewest pieces: big stones, small stones or pieces of thermocol?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will need the fewest pieces to raise the water to the line? Which will need the most? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only what you drop in. Use the same glass, fill it to the same starting line, and use the same top line each time. Drop things in one at a time.
results_table: Guess: how many to reach the line?
Did it ever reach the line?

materials.item: a tall clear glass or plastic tumbler, about 6 to 7 cm across and at least 12 cm tall
water
big stones, each about the size of a walnut, washed. Look in a plant pot, the building compound or the roadside.
small stones, each about the size of a marble, washed. Glass marbles work too.
20 small pieces of thermocol, each about the size of a marble. Break them off the packing from any box.
one flat piece of thermocol about the size of a coin, coloured with a marker, to float as the 'worm'
a marker pen or a strip of tape
a tray or towel for spills

experiments.safety: Wash the stones first. Small children must not put small stones or marbles in their mouths. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Guess. Test big stones, small stones and thermocol. Count and write down the numbers. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each thing you dropped in.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how many objects it took to raise the water to the line
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. The thermocol floated and never reached the line, so we stopped at 20 pieces.

data.label: Thermocol (stopped at 20, never reached the line)

setup.art: A tall clear glass of water on a tray, with one tape line at the water level and a second tape line two finger-widths higher, and a small white thermocol 'worm' floating on the water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the glass to 4 cm below the top. Mark a line 2 cm above the water. Float the 'worm'.

setup.art: A child's hand dropping one big stone into the glass, the water level creeping up.
setup.caption: 2. Drop in big stones, one at a time. Count each one.

setup.art: Three glasses in a row: one with a few big stones, one with many small stones, one with white thermocol pieces floating on top.
setup.caption: 3. Start again with small stones, then thermocol. Which reached the line with the fewest?

flow.do: 1. Fill the glass with water until it is about 4 cm below the top. 2. Put a strip of tape at the water level. This is the starting line. 3. Put a second strip 2 cm higher, about two finger-widths. This is the top line. 4. Float the thermocol 'worm' on the water.
flow.say: Remember the thirsty crow story? The crow dropped pebbles in a pot until it could drink. Let's be the crow. The thermocol is the worm. Our beak can only reach the top line.
flow.kid: Fill the glass. Mark where the water is. Mark a line two fingers higher. Float the worm. Can you bring it up to the line?
flow.parent: Use a glass about 6 to 7 cm across. In a wider glass the water rises too slowly, and you will need many more stones. A steel tumbler works too, but a clear glass lets you see the water rise.
flow.context: This is the first step of the thirsty crow test. You set up a glass of water with a floating 'worm' to raise.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many of each thing they will need. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which do you think will need the fewest: big stones, small stones or thermocol? Why do you think so? Let's write our guesses down first.
flow.kid: Guess first. How many big stones? How many small stones? How many bits of thermocol? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will need the fewest?
good: Big stones take up more room.
Heavy things sink and push the water up.

flow.context: This step of the thirsty crow test is for guessing before you try.

flow.do: Drop in big stones one at a time, counting, until the worm reaches the top line. Write the number. Empty the glass, refill to the starting line, and do the same with small stones. Then do it with the thermocol pieces. Stop the thermocol at 20.
flow.say: One stone at a time. Count out loud. Stop when the worm reaches the line. Now let's empty it and start again, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Drop in one big stone at a time. Count. Stop at the line. Empty the glass. Fill it to the start line. Now try small stones. Then thermocol.
flow.parent: In a glass 6 to 7 cm across, the water must rise 2 cm, so you need to push about 60 to 75 millilitres of water out of the way. A walnut-sized stone takes up about 10 millilitres, so it takes about 5 to 8 big stones. A marble-sized stone takes up only about 2 millilitres, so it takes about 30 to 40 small ones. Thermocol floats and weighs almost nothing, so 20 pieces hardly raise the water at all. This surprises most children.

check.q: In the thirsty crow test, why did the thermocol hardly raise the water?
options: They are too small
It floats, so it does not push much water out of the way
Thermocol soaks up the water
check.why: Things that sink take up room under the water, so the water is pushed up. A floating thing pushes away only as much water as it weighs. Thermocol weighs almost nothing, so it pushes away almost no water. Picking 'too small' usually means thinking only of size, but small stones the same size still worked. Thermocol does not soak up water.

flow.context: This is the main step of the thirsty crow test. You drop in big stones, small stones and pieces of thermocol, and count.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the numbers, with one bar for each thing.
flow.say: Let's turn our numbers into a picture. A short bar means it only took a few. The thermocol never got there, so we stop its bar at 20 and write 'never reached'. Which bar is shortest?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each thing. A short bar means it took only a few. Which bar is shortest?

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many objects it took to raise the water to the line
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. The thermocol floated and never reached the line, so we stopped at 20 pieces.

data.label: Thermocol (stopped at 20, never reached the line)

flow.context: This step of the thirsty crow test turns your counts into a bar chart.

flow.do: Tell your child what real rooks and crows did in this test.
flow.say: In 2009, Christopher Bird and Nathan Emery gave rooks a tube like this. The rooks dropped in stones to reach a floating worm. They chose the big stones first. Later, New Caledonian crows passed similar tests. They chose sinking things over floating ones, just as you found out.
flow.kid: Real rooks did this test! They chose big stones first. Crows picked sinkers, not floaters. Did you?
flow.think: The rooks could not measure or talk it over. How do you think they worked out which stones to use?
flow.context: This step of the thirsty crow test compares your results with what real rooks and crows did.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: big stones raise the water with the fewest pieces. What I saw: it took 6 big stones but 32 small stones, and the thermocol never got there. Why: big sinking stones take up more room under the water, so the water has to go up.
flow.context: This is the last step of the thirsty crow test. The child says what they think, what they saw, and why.

experiments.title: The Clever Hans Test: can you read a face?
experiments.context: This test copies how a horse called Clever Hans was tested in Berlin more than a hundred years ago. Hans seemed to do sums, but he was really reading tiny changes in people's faces. You find out if you can read a face too.
experiments.question: Can you find a hidden coin by watching the face of someone who knows where it is?
experiments.predict: Guess how many times out of 10 you will find the coin when your helper knows where it is. Then guess how many when your helper does not know. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except one thing: whether your helper knows where the coin is. Use the same 3 cups, the same coin and 10 tries each round. Your helper must not speak or point.
results_table: Does the helper know where the coin is?

materials.item: 3 steel cups or tumblers, turned upside down
a coin
3 people: a guesser, a helper who sits facing the guesser, and a hider
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: No safety worries. Keep the coin away from very small children.

schedule.what: Play 10 rounds with a helper who knows, then 10 rounds with a helper who does not. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars: one for 'helper knows' and one for 'helper does not know'.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: right guesses out of 10 in the Clever Hans test
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three upside-down steel cups in a row on a table, a hand slipping a coin under one, while a child at the table has eyes shut.
setup.caption: 1. The hider puts the coin under one cup. The guesser shuts their eyes.

setup.art: A child slowly moving a finger along the three cups while watching the face of a grown-up sitting opposite.
setup.caption: 2. The guesser moves a finger slowly along the cups, watching the helper's face.

setup.art: The same scene, but the grown-up opposite has a scarf tied over their eyes, while another person hides the coin.
setup.caption: 3. Round two: the helper must not know where the coin is.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 cups upside down in a row. 2. The guesser shuts their eyes. 3. The hider puts the coin under one cup, and the helper watches. 4. The helper sits facing the guesser, hands in lap, and says nothing.
flow.say: A horse called Hans seemed to do sums. Really, he watched people's faces. Let's see if you can do what Hans did. Your helper knows where the coin is, but must not speak or point.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. The coin goes under one cup. Your helper knows where. Open your eyes. Watch their face, not the cups!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clever Hans test, where you try to find a hidden coin by reading a face.

flow.do: The guesser moves a finger slowly along the cups, watching the helper's face, then picks one. Do this 10 times, hiding the coin in a new place each time. Count the right guesses.
flow.say: Move your finger slowly over each cup. Keep your eyes on my face. Pick the cup when you feel sure.
flow.kid: Move your finger slowly over the cups. Watch the face. Pick one. Do it 10 times. Count how many you get right.
flow.parent: Helpers should try to keep a still face, but most people still give tiny clues without meaning to. That is exactly what Hans saw.
flow.context: This step of the Clever Hans test is the first round, where the helper knows where the coin is.

flow.do: Now the helper also shuts their eyes or turns away while the hider hides the coin. The hider then leaves the room or turns their back. Play 10 more times and count.
flow.say: Now I won't know where the coin is either. This is called a blind test. Let's see what happens to your score.
flow.kid: Now your helper doesn't know either. This is a blind test. Play 10 more times. Count your right guesses.

check.q: In the Clever Hans test, what usually happens when the helper does not know where the coin is?
options: The guesser gets more right
The guesser gets about the same
The guesser gets fewer right, about 3 out of 10, like lucky guessing
check.why: With 3 cups, a lucky guess is right about 1 time in 3, so about 3 out of 10. When the helper knows, their face gives tiny clues, so scores are often higher. When nobody near knows, the clues disappear. Picking 'more right' usually means not yet seeing that the face was where the clues came from.

flow.context: This step of the Clever Hans test is the blind round, where nobody watching knows where the coin is.

flow.do: Draw two bars, one for each round. Compare them with your guesses.
flow.say: Let's draw our two scores as bars. Was there a difference? Was it big?
flow.kid: Draw two bars. One for 'helper knows'. One for 'blind'. Which is taller?

chart.title: Made-up example results: right guesses out of 10 in the Clever Hans test
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This step of the Clever Hans test turns your two scores into a bar chart.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why did it happen? And why do scientists use blind tests when they test animals?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then say why scientists use blind tests.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: faces give away clues. What I saw: I got 8 right when you knew, and only 3 when you didn't. Why: your face changed a tiny bit at the right cup. Scientists use blind tests so an animal cannot get the answer from them by mistake. If both scores were about the same, that is a real result too. It means your helper kept a very still face.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Clever Hans test. The child says what they think, what they saw, and why.

experiments.title: The Pointing Test: does a dog follow your finger?
experiments.context: This is a test scientists use with dogs. You hide a treat under one of two bowls and point at it. You count how often the dog goes to the right bowl, with pointing and without. You need a calm dog you know well.
experiments.question: Does a dog find a hidden treat more often when a person points at it?
experiments.predict: Guess how many times out of 10 the dog will pick the right bowl with pointing. Then guess without pointing. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: pointing or no pointing. Use the same two bowls, the same spot and the same treat. Rub the treat on both bowls so the dog cannot just smell which one has it.

materials.item: 2 identical steel bowls, turned upside down
small dog treats or bits of dosa
a calm dog you know well, and its owner
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Only use a pet dog, or a dog whose owner is there and says it is calm. Never test an unknown street dog. A grown-up holds the dog's collar between tries. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Play 10 tries with pointing and 10 without. Count and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars: one for 'pointing' and one for 'no pointing'.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: times the dog chose the bowl with the treat, out of 10
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your dog's numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two upside-down steel bowls on a floor about two big steps apart, a child hiding a piece of dosa under one while a grown-up gently holds a dog back.
setup.caption: 1. Hide a treat under one bowl while the dog is held back, facing away.

setup.art: A child kneeling between the bowls, pointing clearly at the left bowl and looking at it, while the dog watches.
setup.caption: 2. Point at the bowl with the treat, and look at it.

setup.art: The dog trotting to the left bowl and nosing it over, the child ticking a chart.
setup.caption: 3. Let the dog go. Which bowl does it choose? Tick the table.

flow.do: 1. Put the two bowls upside down on the floor, about two big steps apart. 2. Rub a treat on both bowls. 3. The owner holds the dog's collar, a few steps back, and turns it away while you hide a treat under one bowl.
flow.say: Scientists test dogs like this all over the world. Let's see if our dog reads our pointing. First, we make sure the dog can't just smell the treat.
flow.kid: Put out two bowls. Rub the treat on both. Hide it under one while the dog looks away.
flow.parent: Choose a calm, friendly dog that knows you. Stop if the dog gets too excited or worried.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pointing test with a dog. You set up two bowls and hide a treat.

flow.do: Kneel between the bowls. Say the dog's name to get its attention. Point clearly at the bowl with the treat and look at it. The owner lets the dog go. Tick right or wrong. Do this 10 times, changing the bowl in a mixed-up order.
flow.say: Watch, I'll say its name, point and look at the bowl. Then let go. Which bowl did it go to?
flow.kid: Say the dog's name. Point at the right bowl and look at it. Let the dog go. Tick right or wrong. Do it 10 times.
flow.context: This step of the pointing test is the round with pointing.

flow.do: Now do 10 more tries without pointing. Just kneel between the bowls and look straight ahead.
flow.say: Now I won't point. If the dog does just as well, what would that tell us?
flow.kid: Now don't point. Look straight ahead. Let the dog go. Tick right or wrong. 10 times.

check.q: In the pointing test, why did we rub the treat on both bowls?
options: To make the bowls taste nice
So the dog cannot find the treat just by smell
To make the dog hungrier
check.why: Dogs have amazing noses. If only one bowl smelled of food, the dog might follow its nose, not your finger. Then we would not be testing pointing at all. Picking 'hungrier' is a kind thought, but it does not make the test fair.

flow.context: This step of the pointing test is the round without pointing, to compare.

flow.do: Draw two bars. Then talk about what scientists found.
flow.say: Brian Hare and his team found that most pet dogs follow pointing. In India, Anindita Bhadra's team at IISER Kolkata found that many street dogs follow pointing too, even though nobody trained them. What did our dog do?
flow.kid: Draw two bars: pointing and no pointing. Most dogs follow pointing. Did yours? Say what you think, what you saw and why.

chart.title: Made-up example results: times the dog chose the bowl with the treat, out of 10
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your dog's numbers will be different.

flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: our dog reads pointing. What I saw: 8 right with pointing, 5 without. Why: dogs watch where people look and point, because they live so closely with us. If your dog did not follow pointing, that is a real result too. Some dogs do and some don't.
flow.context: This is the last step of the pointing test. You draw your results and compare them with what scientists found.

activities.title: Play Spotters
activities.context: In this activity you watch animals for signs of play. Play is doing something just for fun when you are safe. You count each sign you see.

materials.item: a paper with the play signs drawn on it, and a pencil
animals to watch: squirrels, crows or pigeons from a window or balcony, a pet dog or cat, or puppies in your lane

activities.safety: Watch from a distance. Never go close to street dogs, monkeys or cows. Go outdoors only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Watch animals for 10 minutes and tally the play signs.

activities.record: Put a tally mark for each play sign you see. Circle the one you saw most.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five small drawings: a dog doing a play bow, two animals chasing, a jump and twist, an animal tossing a stick, and two animals wrestling gently.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the five play signs on a sheet.

setup.art: A child sitting at a balcony grill watching two palm squirrels chase each other along a ledge, a grown-up beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Watch quietly from a safe distance for 10 minutes.

setup.art: The same sheet with tally marks beside each picture.
setup.caption: 3. Make a tally mark for each sign you see.

flow.do: Draw the five play signs with your child: play bow, chasing, jumping and twisting, tossing a thing, gentle wrestling.
flow.say: Play has signs. A play bow means 'let's play'. Chasing, jumping just for fun, tossing a stick and gentle wrestling are signs too. Let's draw them.
flow.kid: Draw five play signs. A play bow. Chasing. Jumping for fun. Tossing a stick. Gentle wrestling.
flow.context: This is the first step of Play Spotters, where you watch animals for signs of play.

flow.do: Watch animals for 10 minutes. Tally each sign you see.
flow.say: Let's sit very still. Every time you see a play sign, make a mark. Is it play, or is it a real fight? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Sit still and watch. Make a mark for each play sign. Is it play or a real fight?

check.q: Two puppies are rolling and nipping, with loose wagging tails, and they keep swapping who is on top. What is it?
options: A real fight
Play
They are hunting
check.why: In play, animals take turns being on top, their bodies are loose, and nobody gets hurt. In a real fight, bodies are stiff, teeth show and one animal runs away. Picking 'real fight' is a careful guess, because play can look rough.

flow.context: This is the main step of Play Spotters. You watch and count play signs.
flow.parent: Puppies or kittens wrestling are the easiest play to spot. Crows and squirrels chasing each other may be playing, or may be fighting over food. Look for loose bodies and turn-taking. If you see no play in 10 minutes, try again at another time of day, or play with your pet cat or dog and count its play signs.

flow.do: Look at the tallies. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which play sign did you see most? Why do you think the animals were playing?
flow.kid: Which sign did you see most? Why do you think animals play?
flow.parent: A good answer: 'What I think: puppies play to practise fighting. What I saw: 9 chases and 4 play bows. Why: they practised without hurting each other.'
flow.context: This is the last step of Play Spotters. The child looks at their tally and explains it.

activities.title: Be a Jay: hide it, then find it tomorrow
activities.context: Some birds, like jays and nutcrackers, hide seeds and find them months later. In this activity you hide 8 treats and try to find them all the next day, with no map.

materials.item: 8 groundnuts in shells, or 8 small wrapped sweets
one room of your home
a grown-up who secretly writes down where each one is

activities.safety: Do not hide food where ants or pets can get it. Hide nothing near electric plugs or on high shelves.

schedule.what: Hide 8 treats in one room. A grown-up secretly notes where.
Find as many as you can in 3 minutes. Count them.

activities.record: Write how many you found out of 8. Write which ones you forgot.

setup.art: A child tucking a groundnut behind a cushion on a sofa while a grown-up quietly writes on a notepad.
setup.caption: 1. Hide 8 groundnuts around one room. A grown-up notes the spots.

setup.art: A small grey jay pushing a seed into the soil under a pine tree.
setup.caption: 2. Jays do this too, with thousands of seeds.

setup.art: The next day, the child lifting a book to find a groundnut, a sand timer on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Next day: find them in 3 minutes, with no map.

flow.do: Give your child 8 groundnuts. They hide them around one room while you write down where.
flow.say: A bird called a jay hides food and finds it again later. Let's see how good your memory is. Hide these 8 groundnuts. Don't write anything down. Tomorrow you find them.
flow.kid: Hide 8 groundnuts in this room. Don't write anything. Tomorrow you must find them!
flow.context: This is the first day of Be a Jay. You hide 8 treats and try to remember where.

flow.do: The next day, give your child 3 minutes to find them. Count the ones found.
flow.say: Ready? You have 3 minutes. How many can you find? A Clark's nutcracker hides many thousands of seeds, and finds a lot of them months later, even under snow.
flow.kid: You have 3 minutes. Find the groundnuts! How many did you remember?

check.q: In Be a Jay, a child found 6 of 8 groundnuts the next day. A nutcracker bird finds a lot of its many thousands of seeds months later. What does this show?
options: Birds have no memory, they just get lucky
Some birds have amazing memories for places
Children have better memories than all birds
check.why: Scientists moved stones and marks near the hidden seeds, and the birds searched in the wrong place. So the birds use landmarks they remember, not luck or smell. Picking 'lucky' is a fair first guess, but careful tests ruled it out.

flow.context: This is the second day of Be a Jay, when you try to find the hidden treats.

flow.do: Talk about how your child remembered.
flow.say: Which ones did you find first? How did you remember? Did you use the furniture as clues?
flow.kid: How did you remember? Did you use landmarks, like the sofa or the door?
flow.think: Nicola Clayton found that scrub jays remember what they hid, where, and when. Could you remember when you hid each one?
flow.context: This is the last step of Be a Jay. The child explains how they remembered.

activities.title: The Training Game: learning with claps
activities.context: This game shows how animals learn step by step, with rewards. One player is the learner and must find out a secret action. The only clue is a clap each time they get closer.

materials.item: 2 or more players
a small object, like a spoon or a toy

activities.safety: Keep the actions gentle and indoors. No climbing.

schedule.what: Play 3 rounds of the training game, taking turns as trainer and learner.

activities.record: Write how many claps it took each round.

setup.art: A grown-up whispering into a child's ear while another child waits outside the door.
setup.caption: 1. The trainer picks a secret action, like 'put the spoon on the chair'.

setup.art: A child walking towards a chair while the trainer claps once.
setup.caption: 2. The learner moves about. The trainer claps when they get a bit closer.

setup.art: The child placing a spoon on the chair, everyone cheering.
setup.caption: 3. Keep going until the learner does the secret action.

flow.do: Explain the game. The learner leaves the room while the trainer picks a secret action, like 'put the spoon on the chair'.
flow.say: This is how dog and dolphin trainers teach. Karen Pryor, an American dolphin trainer, made this game famous in her book Don't Shoot the Dog in 1984. No words allowed, only claps.
flow.kid: Go outside for a minute. We will choose a secret action. You must find it. The only clue is a clap.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Training Game, a game about how animals learn with rewards.

flow.do: The learner comes back and moves around. The trainer claps each time the learner gets a little closer to the action. No words, no pointing. Play 3 rounds and swap roles.
flow.say: Each clap means 'yes, that's closer'. Watch how the learner figures it out, one small step at a time.
flow.kid: Move around. A clap means you are getting closer. Keep going until you do the secret action.

check.q: In the Training Game, what does each clap teach the learner?
options: That they have finished
That what they just did is a step closer
That they did something wrong
check.why: A clap is a reward that marks the exact moment the learner got closer. Animals learn this way too, one small step at a time. Picking 'did something wrong' mixes up a reward with a telling-off.

flow.context: This is the main part of the Training Game. The learner works out a secret action from claps alone.

flow.do: Talk about how it felt to be the learner.
flow.say: How did it feel to learn without words? How is this like a dog learning to sit?
flow.kid: How did it feel? How is this like a dog learning a trick?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: animals learn in small steps with rewards. What I saw: I got there after 12 claps. Why: each clap told me I was closer.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Training Game. The child says how it felt and links it to animal learning.

activities.title: Reading a Dog: what is it feeling?
activities.context: Dogs read our faces. In this activity you learn to read a dog's face and body, so you can tell if it is happy, scared or angry. This also keeps you safe near dogs.

materials.item: the four dog cards from the app, drawn or printed: relaxed, playful, scared, angry
a pet dog to watch, or photos of dogs

activities.safety: Never touch a dog you do not know. Never run from a dog. If a dog growls, stand still like a tree, arms by your sides, and look away. Tell a grown-up.

schedule.what: Learn the four dog moods. Then sort photos or watch a dog.

activities.record: Draw one dog showing a feeling. Label the tail, ears and mouth.

setup.art: Four dog drawings in a row: relaxed with a loose tail and soft eyes, playful in a play bow, scared with a tucked tail and flat ears, angry with stiff legs and teeth showing.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the four moods: relaxed, playful, scared, angry.

setup.art: A child sorting dog photos into four piles on a mat.
setup.caption: 2. Sort dog pictures into the four moods.

setup.art: A child standing still like a tree, arms by sides, looking away from a growling dog, a grown-up coming.
setup.caption: 3. Practise 'be a tree' for when a dog looks angry.

flow.do: Show the four dog cards. Point out the tail, ears, eyes and mouth on each.
flow.say: Dogs read our faces. We can read theirs too. Look at the tail, the ears, the eyes and the mouth.
flow.kid: Look at the four dogs. Look at each tail, ears and mouth. Which dog is scared?
flow.context: This is the first step of Reading a Dog. You learn four dog moods from tails, ears and faces.

flow.do: Sort dog photos, or watch your own dog, and name each mood.
flow.say: What do you think this dog is feeling? What tells you?
flow.kid: Look at each dog. Name its mood. What told you?

check.q: A dog has its tail tucked between its legs and its ears flat back. What is it probably feeling?
options: Happy
Scared
Hungry
check.why: A tucked tail and flat ears usually mean a dog is scared. A scared dog may snap if you go close, so give it space. Picking 'happy' often comes from thinking any moving tail means happy.

flow.context: This is the main step of Reading a Dog. You name dog moods from pictures or a real dog.

flow.do: Practise 'be a tree': stand still, arms by your sides, look at your feet, and breathe slowly.
flow.say: If a dog ever looks angry or chases you, don't run. Be a tree. Stand still, arms down, look at your feet. The dog usually loses interest.
flow.kid: Practise being a tree. Stand still. Arms down. Look at your feet. Breathe slowly.
flow.parent: In India, children are often around street dogs. This safety habit matters. Any dog bite or scratch needs washing with soap and water for 15 minutes and a doctor the same day, because of rabies.
flow.context: This is the last step of Reading a Dog. You practise a safety habit for when a dog seems angry.

activities.title: Brain Line-up: is bigger cleverer?
activities.context: In this activity you line up kitchen things that are about the size of different animals' brains. Then you find out why the biggest brain is not always the cleverest.

materials.item: a sesame seed
a walnut, or a big amla
a lemon
a medium cauliflower or a medium papaya

activities.safety: No safety worries. Keep the sesame seed away from small children's noses.

schedule.what: Line up the brain-sized objects. Guess which animal is cleverest. Learn about neurons.

activities.record: Draw the line-up. Write the animal next to each object.

setup.art: A sesame seed, a walnut, a lemon and a cauliflower in a row on a steel plate, getting bigger from left to right.
setup.caption: 1. Line up a sesame seed, a walnut, a lemon and a cauliflower.

setup.art: Small drawings of a bee, a crow, a dog and a human head above each object.
setup.caption: 2. Match them: bee, crow, dog, human.

setup.art: A zoom-in circle on the walnut, packed tightly with tiny neuron dots.
setup.caption: 3. Zoom in: a crow's brain is packed with neurons.

flow.do: Line up the objects from smallest to biggest. Tell your child which brain each one is like.
flow.say: A honeybee's brain is smaller than a sesame seed. A crow's is about the size of a walnut. A dog's is about the size of a lemon. Ours weighs about as much as a medium cauliflower.
flow.kid: Line them up, small to big. Bee is the sesame seed. Crow is the walnut. Dog is the lemon. You are the cauliflower.
flow.parent: These sizes are rough. A medium dog's brain is about the size of a lemon. A human brain weighs about 1.3 kg, about as much as a medium cauliflower.
flow.context: This is the first step of Brain Line-up. You compare brain sizes with kitchen things.

flow.do: Tell your child about neurons.
flow.say: Brains are made of tiny messenger cells called neurons. In 2016, scientists counted neurons in bird brains. Crows pack their neurons very tightly. So a crow's walnut brain has about as many neurons in its thinking part as some monkeys. And a bumblebee can learn colours, smells and even to pull a string, with about a million neurons.
flow.kid: Brains are full of tiny cells called neurons. A crow's brain is small, but packed full. So it can be very clever.

check.q: In the Brain Line-up, the crow's brain is like a walnut. Why can crows still make tools?
options: They copy humans
Their small brains are packed tightly with neurons
Tools are easy, so you need no brain
check.why: Bird brains pack neurons very tightly, so a small brain can hold a lot. Picking 'copy humans' is a fair guess, but wild New Caledonian crows make hooks with no humans around.

flow.context: This is the main step of Brain Line-up. You learn that what matters is neurons, not just size.

flow.do: Ask your child what they now think.
flow.say: Is the biggest brain the cleverest? What do you think now, and why?
flow.kid: Is bigger always cleverer? What do you think now? Why?
flow.parent: A good answer: 'What I think: bigger isn't always cleverer. What I saw: the crow's brain is a walnut, but crows make hooks. Why: crows pack in lots of neurons.'
flow.context: This is the last step of Brain Line-up. The child says what they now think about brain size.

activities.title: Mirror, Mirror: who is that?
activities.context: In this activity you try the mirror test on yourself. It is a famous test of whether an animal knows the animal in the mirror is itself.

materials.item: a mirror
a small round sticker or a dot of washable paint

activities.safety: Use washable paint or a sticker only. Keep it away from the eyes.

schedule.what: Put a sticker on your forehead without looking. Use the mirror to find it. Talk about animals and mirrors.

activities.record: Draw yourself in the mirror with the sticker. Write which animals passed the test.

setup.art: A grown-up gently putting a small round sticker on a child's forehead while the child's eyes are shut.
setup.caption: 1. Shut your eyes. A grown-up puts a sticker on your forehead.

setup.art: The child looking into a mirror and touching the sticker on their own forehead.
setup.caption: 2. Look in the mirror. Do you touch your own forehead or the mirror?

setup.art: An elephant at a mirror touching a white cross mark on its own head with its trunk.
setup.caption: 3. Some animals, like Happy the elephant, touched the mark too.

flow.do: Ask your child to shut their eyes. Put the sticker on their forehead. Then let them look in the mirror.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. I'm putting a tiny sticker on your face. Now open your eyes and look in the mirror. What do you do?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. A sticker goes on your face. Now look in the mirror. Where is it?
flow.context: This is the first step of Mirror, Mirror, a try-it-yourself version of the mirror test.

flow.do: Tell your child about the mirror test in animals.
flow.say: Most children pass this test by about age two. In 1970, Gordon Gallup tried it with chimpanzees. They touched the mark. Later, an Asian elephant called Happy did, and so did magpies, a kind of bird. Dogs mostly don't. But dogs know their own smell, and that may be a fairer test for an animal that thinks with its nose.
flow.kid: Chimpanzees, an elephant called Happy and magpies touched the mark. Dogs mostly don't. But dogs know their own smell!

check.q: In the mirror test, a dog ignores the mark on its head. What is the fairest thing to say?
options: Dogs do not know themselves at all
The test may not suit dogs, because dogs use smell more than sight
Dogs cannot see mirrors
check.why: Dogs mostly fail the mirror test, but they sniff their own changed smell for longer. So a test made for eyes may be unfair to an animal that lives by its nose. Picking 'do not know themselves at all' goes further than the evidence.

flow.context: This step of Mirror, Mirror tells which animals pass the mirror test, and why it may be unfair.

flow.do: Ask the big question.
flow.say: When you saw yourself in the mirror, how did you know it was you?
flow.kid: How do you know the child in the mirror is you?
flow.think: Is there a 'you' inside, looking out? Where is it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Mirror, Mirror. It ends with a big question about knowing yourself.

projects.title: Crow Friends: will the crows learn you?
projects.context: In this 7-day project you put out a little plain rice at the same place and time each day, wearing the same cap. You time how long the first crow takes to come. Crows are quick learners, so watch if they start waiting for you.

materials.item: a steel plate
a small handful of plain cooked rice, with no salt or spice, each day
the same bright cap or scarf each day
a watch or phone timer
a notebook and pencil

projects.safety: Feed only a little plain food, so the crows do not depend on you. Do it on a balcony, terrace or yard with a grown-up. Do not touch the birds. Wash the plate and your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Put out the rice in your cap. Time how long until the first crow comes. Write it down.
Same place, same time, same cap. Time the first crow.
Same again. Are crows waiting nearby before you come out?
Same again. Then draw a line chart of all seven days.

projects.record: Write the minutes until the first crow each day. Note how many crows came, and whether any were waiting. Draw a line chart.

setup.art: A child in a bright yellow cap placing a steel plate with a little rice on a balcony ledge, a grown-up nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Same place, same time, same cap: put out a little rice.

setup.art: The child standing back by the door, looking at a phone timer, while a crow lands near the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Step back. Time how long until the first crow comes.

setup.art: A notebook with a line going down across seven days.
setup.caption: 3. Write the minutes each day. Draw a line chart on day 7.

flow.do: On day 1, wear the cap and put out the plate with a little rice. Step back three big steps and start the timer. Stop it when the first crow lands at the plate.
flow.say: Crows learn and remember faces. Let's see if they learn us. Every day we come at the same time, wearing the same cap. We time how long the first crow takes.
flow.kid: Wear your cap. Put out the rice. Step back. Start the timer. Stop it when a crow comes.
flow.parent: Many Indian families already feed crows. Keep the amount small. If no crow comes in 30 minutes, write '30 or more' and try again tomorrow.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Crow Friends, a 7-day project to see whether crows learn who you are.

flow.do: On days 2 to 6, do exactly the same. Write the time each day. Look for crows waiting nearby before you come out.
flow.say: Same place, same time, same cap. Is it getting quicker? Are the crows waiting for us?
flow.kid: Same place. Same time. Same cap. Time the first crow. Is it getting quicker?
flow.wait: Do this once a day, on days 2 to 6.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 6 of Crow Friends. You repeat the same thing each day and time the crows.

flow.do: On day 7, draw a line chart with a dot for each day's minutes, joined by a line.
flow.say: Let's draw our week. Each dot is one day. If the line goes down, the crows came quicker each day.
flow.kid: Put one dot for each day. Join the dots. Does the line go down?

chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until the first crow came, each day
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your crows will be different.

check.q: In Crow Friends, the line went down from 22 minutes on day 1 to 3 minutes on day 7. What is the best explanation?
options: The crows got hungrier
The crows learned when and where food comes
Crows like yellow caps
check.why: The same place, time and cap every day gave the crows a pattern to learn. Coming sooner each day is a sign of learning and memory. Picking 'hungrier' is possible on one day, but not every day for a week. To test the cap, you would need to change only the cap, and keep everything else the same.

flow.context: This is day 7 of Crow Friends. You draw your results as a line chart.

flow.do: Ask your child for claim, evidence and reasoning. Then plan a follow-up test.
flow.say: What do you think the crows learned? What is your evidence? How could we test if they learned your cap, your face or just the time?
flow.kid: What did the crows learn? What is your evidence? How could you test if they know your face?
flow.parent: A good follow-up: wear a different cap, or let someone else come out at the same time, and see if the crows behave differently.
flow.context: This is the last step of Crow Friends. The child explains what the crows learned and plans another test.

challenges.title: Hook It Like Betty
challenges.context: In 2002, a crow called Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a bucket of food out of a tube. In this challenge you try the same thing.
challenges.problem: A tiny paper bucket with a sweet inside sits at the bottom of a tall bottle. Lift it out without tipping the bottle or putting your fingers in.
constraints: You may not tip, shake or cut the bottle.
Your fingers must not go inside the bottle.
You may use only one straight pipe cleaner, or a long strip of kitchen foil rolled tight into a thin stick.
materials: a tall plastic bottle with the top cut off by a grown-up
a tiny paper bucket with a thread handle, made from a paper cup bottom
one pipe cleaner, or a strip of kitchen foil about 30 cm long, rolled tight
general: Bend the end of the pipe cleaner into a hook, and catch the bucket's handle.
Twist the end into a small loop to catch the handle.
creative: Bend a hook at both ends, so you can try again quickly if one misses.
New Caledonian crows also make hooks from twigs, by snapping a branch off just below a fork. Could you make a hook from a forked twig?
What if you could only use your mouth, like Betty? Try holding the pipe cleaner in a clothes peg instead of your fingers.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own tool. Draw it, make it and test it. How many tries did it take?

setup.art: A tall cut-off plastic bottle with a tiny paper bucket and thread handle sitting at the bottom, a straight pipe cleaner lying beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put the paper bucket with a sweet at the bottom of the bottle.

setup.art: A child's hands bending the end of a pipe cleaner into a hook shape.
setup.caption: 2. Bend the pipe cleaner into a tool.

setup.art: The hook lifting the bucket by its thread handle out of the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Hook the handle and lift the bucket out.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the top off a tall plastic bottle. Make a tiny bucket from the bottom of a paper cup, with a thread handle. Put a sweet in it and drop it to the bottom.
flow.say: A crow called Betty did this in Oxford in 2002. She had a straight wire and a bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. Let's see if you can do what Betty did.
flow.kid: The sweet is at the bottom. No fingers inside! You only have a straight pipe cleaner.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hook It Like Betty, a challenge to make a tool like a clever crow.

flow.do: Let your child try. Do not tell them to make a hook. Count the tries.
flow.say: Try it. If the straight one doesn't work, what could you change about it?
flow.kid: Try to lift the bucket. Does a straight pipe cleaner work? What can you change?

check.q: In Hook It Like Betty, why does a straight pipe cleaner fail?
options: It is too short
It has nothing to catch the handle
It is too soft
check.why: A straight stick just slides past the handle. A hook catches it. Betty seemed to see this and bent the wire. Picking 'too short' usually means the bottle is very tall, so check the length first.

flow.context: This is the main step of Hook It Like Betty. The child tries to make a working tool.

flow.do: Talk about what Betty did, and compare.
flow.say: Betty bent the wire into a hook, and lifted the bucket. Later, scientists found wild crows bend twigs too. So some think Betty used a skill crows already have, in a new way. How many tries did you need?
flow.kid: Betty made a hook. Did you? How many tries did it take? Was it harder than you thought?
flow.think: Is making a tool a sign of thinking? What else could explain it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hook It Like Betty. You compare your tool with Betty's.

challenges.title: Build a Puzzle Feeder
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a puzzle that a pet or a bird must solve to get a treat. Zoos and pet owners do this to keep animal minds busy and happy.
challenges.problem: Make a feeder from things at home that a pet, or crows on the balcony, must think about to get a treat. It must be safe, and it must be possible to solve.
constraints: Use only safe things: cardboard, paper, cloth, steel cups. No string loops that could catch a neck or a beak.
The animal must be able to solve it in under 5 minutes.
No sharp edges, glue or tape where the animal will touch.
materials: a cardboard egg tray or small boxes
small treats for a pet, or a little plain rice for birds
general: Hide treats in an egg tray and cover each one with a crumpled paper ball.
Roll treats inside a towel, so the animal must unroll it.
Put a treat under one of three paper cups.
creative: Bumblebees learned to pull a string to drag a fake flower out from under a plastic sheet. They even learned by watching other bees. Could a bird learn to pull a cloth tab to slide a plate out?
Make a puzzle with two steps, like lifting a flap and then pushing a ball.
Make the puzzle a little harder each day, and time how long it takes.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own puzzle. Draw it, build it and watch who solves it. Time how long it takes. Does it get faster on the second day?

setup.art: A cardboard egg tray with crumpled paper balls in each cup and a few treats hidden underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Hide treats in an egg tray under paper balls.

setup.art: A dog nosing a paper ball out of an egg tray to find a treat.
setup.caption: 2. Let the animal find the treats. Time it.

setup.art: A child drawing a new puzzle design with flaps and a sliding plate.
setup.caption: 3. Design a harder puzzle. Does the animal get faster?

flow.do: Build a simple puzzle, like the egg tray with paper balls.
flow.say: Clever animals get bored. Zoos give them puzzles so their minds stay busy. Let's build one.
flow.kid: Build a puzzle feeder. Hide treats under paper balls in an egg tray.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Puzzle Feeder, a challenge to make a puzzle for an animal.

flow.do: Put it out for a pet, or for crows on the balcony. Watch from a distance and time how long it takes.
flow.say: Let's step back and watch. Is the animal trying different things? Is it getting quicker?
flow.kid: Step back. Watch quietly. Time it. What does the animal try first?

check.q: In Build a Puzzle Feeder, the dog took 3 minutes on day 1 and 1 minute on day 2. What does that show?
options: The dog learned and remembered how to solve it
The puzzle got easier by itself
The dog was not hungry on day 1
check.why: Getting faster at the same puzzle is a sign of learning and memory. Picking 'not hungry' could be true for one day, so a scientist would test on more days to be sure.

flow.context: This is the main step of Build a Puzzle Feeder. You watch an animal solve the puzzle and time it.

items.p: What is learning?
opts: Being born knowing how to do something
Changing what you do because of what happened before
items.why: Learning means you change what you do after something happens, like a dog running to the gate when it clicks. Picking 'born knowing' mixes learning up with instinct, which needs no teaching.

items.p: Which of these is play?
opts: Two puppies chasing each other with wagging tails
A cat running from a big dog
items.why: Play is done for fun, when safe and relaxed. Eating, running from danger and nest building all have a job to do right now. Picking 'running from a big dog' means a chase was seen as play, but that cat is scared, not relaxed.

items.p: An object an animal uses to help it do a job is called a ____.
items.why: A crow's twig hook and a chimpanzee's grass stem are both tools.

items.p: Only humans use tools.
items.why: Chimpanzees, crows, Egyptian vultures and sea otters use tools. Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees fishing for termites in 1960.

items.p: Match each animal to what scientists saw it do.
pairs: bent a wire into a hook
fished for termites with a grass stem
items.why: Each of these was found in careful tests or long watching by scientists.

items.p: Sort these. Is it LEARNED or INSTINCT (born knowing)?
items: a baby turtle walking to the sea
a crow avoiding a person who once scared it
a spider spinning its first web
a cow coming home at the same time each evening
items.why: Learned things come from experience. Instinct is there from birth, with no teaching. A spider's first web is not taught.

items.p: A dog has its tail tucked under and its ears flat back. How is it probably feeling?
items.why: A tucked tail and flat ears usually mean fear. Give a scared dog space. Picking 'playful' often comes from expecting dogs always to be happy.

items.p: A test where the person giving it does not know the answer is called a ____ test.
items.why: In a blind test, nobody nearby can give away the answer by mistake, like the people who asked Clever Hans did.

items.p: Clever Hans the horse seemed to do sums. What was he really doing?
opts: Reading tiny changes in the asker's face and body
items.why: Hans stopped tapping when the asker relaxed a tiny bit at the right number. He was right only when the asker knew the answer. Picking 'counting' means trusting the trick without a blind test.
items.context: This question is about Clever Hans, a horse in Berlin more than a hundred years ago, who seemed to tap out answers to sums with his hoof.

items.p: Which bird hides thousands of seeds and finds many of them months later?
items.why: The Clark's nutcracker hides thousands of pine seeds in autumn and finds a lot of them in winter, using landmarks it remembers.

items.p: Crows can remember a human face for years.
items.why: In John Marzluff's study, crows scolded a 'dangerous' mask for years, and young crows learned it from older ones.

items.p: The thirsty crow test: after 6 big stones the water reached the line. After 32 small stones it reached the line too. The big stones took ____ fewer objects.
items.why: 32 take away 6 is 26. So the big stones took 26 fewer objects. You can check: 6 + 26 = 32.
items.context: This question is about the thirsty crow test. You drop things into a glass of water, one at a time, and count how many it takes to raise the water to a line near the top.

items.p: Draw a crow using a tool. Label the tool and what the crow wants to get.
items.a: A crow holding a twig or wire hook in its beak, reaching into a hole or tube, with a grub or food labelled.
items.why: A tool is something outside the body used to help do a job.
items.art: An empty box with a branch drawn at the edge.

items.p: Why did we rub the treat on both bowls in the dog pointing test?
opts: So both bowls smell the same, and the dog must use our pointing
So the dog gets two treats
items.why: Dogs have powerful noses. If only one bowl smelled of food, the dog could follow its nose instead of the pointing. Picking 'two treats' misses the point of a fair test.
items.context: This question is about the pointing test. A treat is hidden under one of two bowls, and a person points at it to see if a dog follows the point.

items.p: Tell about one animal that plays. What does it do, and why do you think it plays?
items.a: Any true example, for example: puppies chase and wrestle. I think they are practising for real life and making friends.
items.why: Scientists have several ideas about why animals play: practice, friendship, coping with surprises, and fun.

items.p: Put these in order, smallest brain to biggest: crow, honeybee, human, dog.
items.why: A bee brain is smaller than a sesame seed, a crow's is about a walnut, a dog's is about a lemon, and ours weighs about as much as a medium cauliflower. But size alone does not tell you how clever an animal is.

items.p: In the Clever Hans test, the guesser got 8 out of 10 when the helper knew, and 3 out of 10 when the helper did not know. What does this show?
opts: The helper's face gave clues without meaning to
items.why: When the helper knew, tiny face changes gave clues. Without them, the guesser was only lucky about 1 time in 3. Picking 'lucky coin' misses that the only thing changed was whether the helper knew.
items.context: This question is about the Clever Hans test. A guesser tries to find a coin under one of 3 cups by watching a helper's face. In one round the helper knows where the coin is. In the other, the helper does not know.

items.p: With 3 cups, a lucky guess is right about 1 time in ____.
items.why: There are 3 cups and one coin, so a random pick is right about 1 time in 3. In 10 tries, that is about 3 right.
items.context: This question is about the Clever Hans test. A guesser tries to find a coin under one of 3 cups by watching a helper's face. In one round the helper knows where the coin is. In the other, the helper does not know.

items.p: In the thirsty crow test, which object should a clever crow choose?
items.why: Sinking things take up room under the water and push it up. Big stones push up the most. Floating things like thermocol, feathers and leaves barely raise the water. Rooks chose big stones first.
items.context: This question is about the thirsty crow test. You drop things into a glass of water, one at a time, and count how many it takes to raise the water to a line near the top.

items.p: A bigger brain always means a cleverer animal.
items.why: Elephants and whales have bigger brains than us. Crows have small brains packed with neurons, and they make tools. What matters is more than size.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: chimpanzees make tools from grass stems
jays remember what, where and when
many street dogs in India follow pointing
items.why: Each of these scientists watched or tested animals carefully. Jane Goodall, Nicola Clayton and Anindita Bhadra are women who changed how we see animal minds.
items.context: This question is about four scientists from this unit who studied animal minds.

items.p: Alexandra Horowitz tested the 'guilty look' of dogs in 2009. What did she find?
opts: Dogs look guilty only when they did something wrong
Dogs looked most 'guilty' when the owner scolded them, even if they had done nothing wrong
items.why: The look seemed to follow the owner's scolding, not the dog's actions. So it may mean 'please don't be angry'. Picking the first answer is what most owners believe, which is why the test was needed.
items.context: Many dog owners say their dog looks guilty after chewing a chappal. This question is about a test of that idea.

items.p: Sort these. Is it LEARNING, MEMORY, PLAY or TOOL USE?
items: a jay finding seeds it hid months ago
a bumblebee rolling a ball for no reward
a sea otter cracking a shell on a stone
a dog getting faster at a puzzle feeder
a chimpanzee fishing termites with a stem
goats leaping and twisting in a field
items.why: Learning changes what an animal does, memory keeps it, play is for fun, and tool use means using an outside object for a job.

items.p: Crow Friends project: on day 1 the first crow came after 22 minutes. On day 7 it came after 3 minutes. That is ____ minutes faster.
items.why: 22 take away 3 is 19. The crows came 19 minutes sooner. You can check: 3 + 19 = 22.
items.context: This question is about the Crow Friends project. Each day for 7 days, a child put out a little rice at the same place and time, wearing the same cap, and timed how long the first crow took to come.

items.p: In the Crow Friends project, what would be a fair test of whether crows know your cap?
opts: Change the time and the place and the cap
Keep the time and place the same, and wear a different cap
items.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. If the crows act differently with a new cap, the cap mattered. Changing everything at once makes it impossible to tell which change mattered.
items.context: This question is about the Crow Friends project, where a child puts out rice each day at the same place and time, wearing the same cap.

items.p: Clever Hans could not do sums. Was he clever? Give your reason.
items.a: Any reasoned answer, for example: yes, because he could read tiny face changes that people did not even know they made.
items.why: Reading faces is a real skill. The story shows animals can be clever in ways we do not think to test.
items.context: Clever Hans was a horse in Berlin who seemed to do sums, but was really reading people's faces.

items.p: An octopus has about two thirds of its neurons in its arms. What does this mean?
opts: Its arms can feel, taste and grab partly on their own
Its arms are made of brain
items.why: The arms have so many neurons that each can explore partly on its own. The octopus still has a brain in its head. Picking 'no brain' goes too far.

items.p: Scientists all agree that insects feel pain.
items.why: Scientists still argue about it. Some tests show bees and crabs act in pain-like ways, but nobody knows for sure what they feel.

items.p: Brian Hare's team found that pet dogs follow pointing better than chimpanzees. Why might that be?
opts: Dogs have lived with people for thousands of years
Dogs have bigger brains than chimpanzees
items.why: Dogs have lived alongside people for a very long time, and grow up watching us. Dogs do not have bigger brains than chimpanzees. Chimpanzees can see fingers fine, but are less tuned to follow them.

items.p: Draw the four dog moods: relaxed, playful, scared and angry. Show the tail and ears on each.
items.a: Relaxed: loose tail, soft ears. Playful: play bow, tail up. Scared: tail tucked, ears flat. Angry: stiff body, teeth showing, tail stiff.
items.why: Dogs show feelings with tails, ears, mouths and bodies. Reading them keeps you safe.
items.art: Four empty boxes, each with a dog outline.

items.p: Put the steps of the thirsty crow test in order.
items: Fill the glass, and mark the starting line and a top line 2 cm higher
Guess how many objects you will need
Drop objects in one at a time and count
Write the number and draw a bar chart
items.why: Set up first, then guess, then test, then record. Guessing first keeps you honest.
items.context: This question is about the thirsty crow test. You drop things into a glass of water, one at a time, and count how many it takes to raise the water to a line near the top.

items.p: Neurons pass signals using charged atoms of which substances?
opts: Sodium and potassium, like in salt and bananas
Iron and copper, like in wires
items.why: Neuron signals are made by charged sodium and potassium atoms moving in and out of the cell. Picking 'iron and copper' comes from thinking of electric wires, but the brain's electricity is carried by salts in water.

items.p: Your brain has about 86 ____ neurons.
items.why: About 86 billion. Suzana Herculano-Houzel and her team counted them by dissolving brains into a soup and counting the cell centres.

items.p: Our last shared ancestor with octopuses lived more than 500 million years ago, and was a small worm-like animal. What does this suggest?
opts: Clever minds grew more than once, on different branches of life
items.why: Octopuses and crows became clever on very different branches from us. So minds may have grown up at least twice. Picking 'close cousins' misses how long ago we split.

items.p: Descartes said animals are like clever machines with no feelings. Darwin said animals have feelings like ours. Who do you agree with? Give one piece of evidence.
items.a: Any answer with evidence, for example: Darwin, because dogs show fear with their bodies and avoid pain, just as we do.
items.why: This is still argued about. Good answers use evidence, not just opinion.
items.context: This question is about two thinkers who disagreed about whether animals feel: Rene Descartes in 1637 and Charles Darwin in 1872.

items.p: Why might the mirror test be unfair to dogs?
opts: Dogs live mainly by smell, so a test for eyes may miss what they know
Dogs are too big for mirrors
items.why: Alexandra Horowitz showed dogs know their own smell. A test that suits one animal's senses may not suit another's. Picking 'too big' misses the real problem: the test uses sight.

items.p: A bumblebee rolled balls even when there was no food reward.
items.why: Scientists in London found this in 2022. Young bees rolled balls the most. It looks a lot like play.

items.p: Match each tool to its user.
pairs: stone thrown at an ostrich egg
items.why: Tool use has been found in many very different animals, not just apes.

items.p: Thirsty crow test: 6 big stones raised the water to the line. How many would you need to do it twice, in two glasses? ____
items.why: 6 stones for each glass, and 2 glasses. 6 + 6 = 12, or 2 times 6 is 12.
items.context: This question is about the thirsty crow test. You drop things into a glass of water, one at a time, and count how many it takes to raise the water to a line near the top.

items.p: Conwy Lloyd Morgan said: choose the simplest explanation that fits. A cat opens a door by pulling the handle. What is the simplest explanation?
opts: It learned by trying, and pulling the handle worked
items.why: The simplest explanation is learning by trying, like Thorndike's cats in puzzle boxes. Picking 'understands hinges' may be true, but we would need more tests to show it.

items.p: The New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness, 2024, said there is a real chance insects have feelings. If so, should we change how we treat insects? Explain.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer, for example: we could avoid hurting insects for no reason, like not pulling wings off.
items.why: When we are not sure whether a being can feel, many people think it is wise to be careful and kind.
items.context: In 2024, many scientists signed a statement saying mammals and birds very likely have feelings, and fish, octopuses, crabs and insects might too.

items.p: Pigeons learned to tell paintings by Monet from paintings by Picasso, even new ones they had never seen. What does this show?
opts: Pigeons can learn general patterns, not just single pictures
items.why: The pigeons sorted new paintings correctly, so they had learned a pattern of style. Picking 'love art' is fun, but the test measured learning, not liking.

items.p: Most children pass the mirror test by about age two.
items.why: Babies younger than about 18 months usually do not touch the mark. By about two years old, most do.

items.p: Clever Hans was right only when the asker knew the answer. Which kind of test showed this?
items.why: In a blind test, the asker did not know the answer. Then Hans failed. That showed the answer came from the asker's face and body.
items.context: Clever Hans was a horse in Berlin who seemed to do sums by tapping his hoof.

items.p: Draw what you think is happening inside a crow's brain as it bends a wire. Show neurons passing a signal.
items.a: A crow's head with many tiny neurons joined by lines, with sparks or arrows moving along them.
items.why: In a brain, every thought comes with neurons passing tiny electric signals to each other. Drawing a model helps us picture what we cannot see.
items.art: An empty outline of a crow's head.

items.p: Write one question about animal minds that nobody knows the answer to yet.
items.a: Any honest open question, for example: what does it feel like to be a bee? Do fish feel happy?
items.why: Science grows from good open questions.

opts: Bumblebees rolling little balls with no reward

opts: Bent a straight wire into a hook to get food
quiz.why: Betty bent a wire into a hook to lift a tiny bucket of food from a tube.

quiz.p: What did Jane Goodall see a chimpanzee do in 1960?
opts: Poke a grass stem into a termite mound to fish out termites
quiz.why: This showed humans are not the only tool makers. Picking 'build a house' is a guess with no evidence.

quiz.p: A person points at one of two bowls. What do most pet dogs do?
opts: Go to the bowl the person pointed at
Look at the finger and do nothing
Always go to the left bowl
quiz.why: Most dogs follow pointing. Many untrained street dogs in India do too.

quiz.p: Scientists showed dogs photos of human faces. What could the dogs learn to tell apart?
quiz.why: In 2015, dogs in Vienna learned to tell happy from angry faces, even of strangers.

quiz.p: In the thirsty crow test, why must we fill the glass to the same starting line each time?
opts: To make it a fair test
quiz.why: If the water starts at different levels, we cannot compare the counts. Change only one thing at a time.

quiz.p: Clever Hans got sums wrong when the asker did not know the answer. Why?
opts: He could no longer read the answer from the asker's face
quiz.why: Hans read tiny relaxations in the asker's face. With no answer to give away, he had no clue. This is why scientists use blind tests.

opts: A test with your eyes shut
A test where the person giving it does not know the answer
A test done in the dark
quiz.why: In a blind test, nobody nearby can give clues by mistake. Picking 'eyes shut' takes the word 'blind' too literally.

quiz.p: Which statement do most scientists agree on?
opts: Many animals learn, remember and solve problems
Insects definitely feel exactly what we feel
quiz.why: Learning and memory are tested and agreed. What insects feel is still argued about.

opts: Whether fish and insects feel pain
quiz.why: Crow tools and dog learning are well tested. Feelings in fish and insects are still debated.

quiz.p: A crow's brain is about the size of a walnut. How can crows be so clever?
opts: Their brains are packed tightly with neurons
quiz.why: Bird brains pack neurons tightly, so a small brain holds a lot. Brain size alone does not tell you how clever an animal is.

opts: Tiny messenger cells that pass electric signals
quiz.why: Neurons pass tiny signals made by charged atoms moving. In a brain, every thought and memory comes with neurons signalling.

applications: Dog trainers and guide-dog schools use reward training, the same learning seen in the Training Game.
Police and army dogs sniff out bombs and lost people, using learning and memory.
Zoos give animals puzzle feeders so their minds stay busy and they stay healthy.
Farmers who understand animal feelings keep calmer, healthier cows and hens.
Scientists use blind tests, from the Clever Hans lesson, when testing medicines on people too.
Robot makers study octopus arms to build soft robot arms that can grip things gently.
Laws in India, like the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, protect animals because they can suffer.
Doctors study animal memory to understand memory loss in people.
Elephants follow old routes they remember, so wildlife workers protect those routes as safe corridors between forests.
Bird counts, like those run by Bird Count India, depend on people who watch birds carefully and know their habits.
