open_questions.q: What does it feel like to be a crow, a bee or an octopus?
open_questions.why_open: We can test what animals do, but we cannot get inside their experience. The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked 'What is it like to be a bat?' in 1974, and it is still unanswered.

open_questions.q: Do fish, crabs and insects feel pain?
open_questions.why_open: They act in pain-like ways in some tests, but their brains are very different from ours. Scientists still argue.
There are several good ideas: practice, friendship, coping with surprises, and fun. Nobody knows how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: How do tiny neurons passing signals become a feeling or a memory?
open_questions.why_open: We can see neurons fire, but nobody knows how that becomes the feeling of being happy. This is called the hard problem of consciousness.
The mirror test suits animals that use eyes. Scientists are still looking for fair tests for animals that live by smell or sound.

open_questions.q: Did dogs become good at reading people because of their genes, or by growing up with us?
open_questions.why_open: Tests of wolves, pet dogs and street dogs give different answers. Probably both matter.

open_questions.q: How did intelligence grow up separately in crows, octopuses and apes?
open_questions.why_open: Their brains are built very differently, yet all solve problems. Scientists are still working out what they share.

maths.problem: In Be a Jay, Arjun hid 8 groundnuts. The next day he found 6. What fraction did he find? How many did he forget?
maths.answer: He found 6 out of 8, which is three quarters. He forgot 2.
maths.explain: 8 take away 6 is 2, so he forgot 2. 6 out of 8 is the same as 3 out of 4, because 6 and 8 can both be halved. So he found three quarters.
maths.context: This is about Be a Jay. You hide 8 treats in a room, then try to find them the next day with no map, like a bird that hides seeds.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how good a memory is, even when people hide different numbers of things.

maths.problem: In the pointing test, a dog chose the right bowl 8 times out of 10 with pointing, and 5 times out of 10 with no pointing. Draw a tally for each round. How many more right choices did pointing give?
maths.explain: With pointing, the tally is 8 marks. With no pointing, it is 5 marks. 8 take away 5 is 3. With 2 bowls, a lucky guess is right about 5 times in 10, so the no-pointing score is about luck.
maths.context: This is about the pointing test. A treat is hidden under one of two bowls, and a person points at it, or does not, to see if a dog follows the point.

roots.context: We have been learning that animals play, learn, remember and read faces. Now we ask what that tells us about minds, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your glass, big stones raised the water with the fewest pieces, and you could say why. Rooks given a tube of water also chose big stones first, though they cannot tell us why. Nobody can see inside another mind, so we judge even a friend's mind by what they do. Judged the same way, the rook was thinking, just as you were.
deep_truth.habit: We accept that a friend thinks because of what they do and say. For animals we often ask for much more proof. That uses one rule for people and a stricter one for every other animal.
deep_truth.evidence: In 2009, Christopher Bird and Nathan Emery gave rooks a tube with a worm floating out of reach. The rooks dropped in stones until they could eat it, and they picked big stones first. In the thirsty crow test, you found the same thing: big sinking stones raise the water with the fewest pieces.

three.who_am_i: You are one of many minds on Earth. A crow, a dog and you all learn, remember and decide.
three.what_is_life: Living things notice, learn, remember and choose. Crows, dogs, octopuses and you all do this, with very different bodies.
three.what_is_this_world: A crow, a dog and a bee notice different things in the same street. Each of them lives in its own version of the world.

roots.thread: A crow, a dog and you look very different from outside. Inside, your thinking and theirs runs on neurons passing signals with the same sodium and potassium atoms. Clever minds came about separately in crows, octopuses and apes, on branches of life that split long ago. Awareness runs through all of life, so it keeps showing up wherever life goes, in a bird, a dog or an eight-armed octopus.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 17 (Autumn Floods), the fish of the Hao river
teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi stood on a bridge. Zhuangzi said, 'See how the fish swim about. That is their joy.' Huizi said, 'You are not a fish. How do you know what fish enjoy?' Zhuangzi said, 'You are not me. How do you know I don't know?'
teachings.link: Huizi could not see inside Zhuangzi's mind either, yet he argued with him as a mind. We know every other mind, a friend's or a fish's, from what it does.

teachings.teaching: One who sees all beings in their own self, and their own self in all beings, does not hate anyone.
teachings.link: When we see that a crow learns and a dog feels, we start to see ourselves in them, and them in us.

science.text: Many animals learn, remember, play and solve problems. This has been tested many times.
Many scientists agree that mammals and birds very likely have feelings. For fish, octopuses, crabs and insects, many see a real chance, and the tests go on.

other_view.who: Many careful scientists, following Conwy Lloyd Morgan, and the philosopher Rene Descartes before them
other_view.view: We should not read human feelings into animals. A crow bending a hook may be following simple learned rules, with nothing it is like inside. Descartes went further and said animals feel nothing at all. Most scientists today disagree with Descartes, but many still warn against seeing a mind like ours in every animal. That is an honest and careful view.

practice.title: Be a quiet watcher
practice.say: Let's sit by the window, or near a pet, and be very still. Pick one animal, a crow, a pigeon, a dog or even an ant. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Just watch it for one minute without talking. Now imagine looking out through its eyes. What does it see? What might it want? Then come back to your own eyes, and breathe once more.
practice.kid: Sit very still. Pick one animal to watch. Breathe slowly. Watch it for one minute. Imagine looking out through its eyes. Then come back to you.

how_we_found_out.story: For about a hundred years, scientists thought birds were poor thinkers. Around 1900, a German brain scientist called Ludwig Edinger studied bird brains. He decided that most of a bird's forebrain matched a part of our brain thought to run instincts. The part we think with, the wrinkled outer layer called the cortex, seemed to be almost missing in birds. So for a long time, books said birds act mostly on instinct, and 'bird brain' became a word for a silly person. Then birds kept surprising scientists. In 2002, a crow called Betty bent a wire into a hook. Crows remembered faces, and jays remembered where and when they hid food. In the early 2000s, a group of scientists, including Erich Jarvis and Anton Reiner, looked at bird brains again. They found that most of a bird's forebrain does the same job as our cortex, only arranged in clumps instead of layers. So they gave its parts new names in 2004. In 2016, scientists counted the neurons. A crow's small forebrain held about as many as some monkeys have.
how_we_found_out.who: Ludwig Edinger first, then Erich Jarvis, Anton Reiner and many others, and later Suzana Herculano-Houzel's team, who counted the neurons
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Birds have almost no thinking part in their brains, so they act mostly on instinct. A closer look showed that most of a bird's forebrain does the job of our cortex, and in 2016 neuron counts showed that crows pack in as many as some monkeys.
